item.title: Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dnrpmgv4yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away - Published The changing room is busy with footballers going through their pre-match routines. Some stretch and tighten their boots, others embrace. "Be strong as always because we are representing Afghan women," says midfielder Fatima Haidari to fellow members of Afghan Women United. Applause erupts in the room where an Afghan flag hangs and a patriotic song is played. As the women sing along some struggle to hold back tears. There's a final team huddle with words of encouragement from their coach before they head out to the pitch – a place that for years they had been told they did not belong. The 23-player squad, selected from Afghan players now living abroad, has travelled to New Zealand for a training camp and to play two unofficial friendly games against the Cook Islands. This is the first time they have been together since football governing body Fifa ruled in April that they could represent their country in official matches in the future. Previously, they would have needed the approval of the Afghanistan Football Federation. This was not possible under the Taliban, who returned to power in August 2021, imposing wide-ranging restrictions on women and girls, including barring them from secondary school and university, most professions and organised sport. The country's national women's team, formed in 2007, could no longer play and its members were among those evacuated and resettled in countries including Australia, the UK and Portugal. Years of campaigning led to the creation of a refugee team, which became Afghan Women United. Thanks to Fifa's ruling, it can now try to qualify for international competitions such as the Olympics and World Cup. Gathered in New Zealand, the squad is excited to be playing together - as asylum seekers living in various countries it has been hard for them to get the travel documents in order to train as a team over the past five years. Sitting in the hotel in Auckland the day before the match, Manozh Noori, who has short hair, wears a T-shirt and knee-length shorts - a look that she says has often drawn criticism from relatives for looking too masculine. As the 23-year-old speaks to BBC Global Women about her family, her voice begins to falter. She pauses, takes a deep breath and looks away for a moment before continuing. There are no tears, but the emotion is clear. Noori now lives in Australia but she grew up playing football with boys in the streets of Kabul. After seeing women's football on television, she secretly joined local clubs and gradually rose through the ranks in Afghanistan. She knew her older brother would disapprove so she tried to reduce the risk of being recognised by wearing a face covering. Over six years, she won league titles, national championships and individual awards. Eventually her success became impossible to hide. In about 2018 her fellow players persuaded her to remove her face covering for a TV interview, which was shown on the news along with highlights of their match. Then she had to face the reality that her brother might see it. "I was so scared," she recalls. "I kept thinking, 'He's going to see me. He's going to know.'" In desperation, she tried to stop the family from watching the news by turning off the electricity, but word soon reached her brother and he was furious, she says. "He was screaming," Noori says. "'You told us you were studying. You said you wanted to become a teacher or a doctor. What is this?'" He threatened to cut his ties with the family if she didn't stop, she adds. "My mother was crying. She told me, 'He's the person who supports us financially. How are we going to survive?'" Noori did stop playing for a while, but eventually started again. She says her other brother, who lives in Germany, sent money to help finance her dream. When the Taliban took over in 2021, Noori decided to flee, but first she buried her football medals and trophies in the garden of her family home. More than four years later, they remain there. "One day I will go back and dig them out," she says, briefly smiling at the thought. "Football helped me get my mum and sister out of Afghanistan," she says. Two years after she moved to Australia and established herself as a football player, she was able to bring them over as well. This meant her sister was able to study again - even though her brother didn't want them playing sports, he always supported their education. "I hope my brother now realises I am not a bad person," says Noori. Afghan Reunited: The fight for football BBC Global Women follows Afghan female footballers as they return to the pitch As she and the team prepare for the matches in Auckland, many of them describe football as the reason they survived one of the most turbulent periods in their country's recent history. "If I wasn't a footballer, I would still be in Afghanistan, one of millions of girls who are not allowed to study, speak up or choose their own future," says Mursal Sadat, who also lives in Australia. Now 24, she works as a football coach, youth facilitator and advocate for refugees, women's rights and human rights. In Afghanistan, she says she was often judged, harassed and told that no-one would want to marry a woman who played sport. Today she is engaged to a man who is still in Afghanistan, and says he and his family are supportive of her work and place on the national team. "They tell me, 'You are the pride of our family. We are so lucky to have you.'" As the players step out into the driving Auckland rain to face the Cook Islands, they channel their energy and determination, unfazed by the weather. They have faced much tougher conditions back home. As a teenager, defender Najma Arefi trained in temperatures above 45C (113F) because girls were often given the least desirable training slots. Still, she persisted. The 22-year-old's efforts eventually helped a Herat-based team win a national championship. The victory, she says, changed attitudes towards women's sport in the city. "There were billboards of us across Herat," she recalls. "People were proud. More families started letting their daughters play football." She now lives in Doncaster in northern England. She arrived in the UK after the Taliban takeover. She describes herself as an extrovert and says she now has opportunities she never imagined growing up in Afghanistan. She studies criminal justice at college, plays football and makes decisions independently. "Having that freedom is incredible," she says. Yet she admits she often feels guilty and desperately sad about the freedoms denied to women back home. "Millions of girls don't have the chance to study or follow their dreams. I feel I have to make the most of every opportunity. "Sometimes I put too much pressure on myself," she says, tears rolling down her face. She thanks Khalida Popal, who founded the original Afghan women's team, for pushing Fifa to recognise them now they are in exile. "To receive Fifa's recognition without the approval of the Taliban" has made history, she says. This official status is "something I'll always be proud of", she says. When the BBC asked the Taliban's director for sports, Ahmadullah Wasiq, about Fifa backing the women's team, he declined to comment. But he said he would like Fifa to visit the country and resume its support for football there in general - the organisation largely withdrew after the Taliban came to power. Fifa has previously said any resumption of support would depend on women being allowed to play. The game in Auckland turns out to be unforgiving. A single goal in the first match hands the Cook Islands a 1-0 victory. Three days later, despite the Afghan team's best efforts, the Cook Islands win again, this time 3-0. Yet for the players, these matches represent something far more significant than two defeats. A return to the pitch and proof that despite exile, separation from their families and years of uncertainty, Afghanistan's women footballers refused to disappear. - This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

item.title: El-Sayed's victory sends tremors through Democratic Party
item.description:

========================================
El-Sayed's victory sends tremors through Democratic Party - Published The tremors from Abdul El-Sayed's victory in Michigan's Senate primary will have been felt hundreds of miles away by the Democratic Party leadership. In a year in which Republicans appear to be facing significant electoral headwinds, Democratic primary voters have taken a chance on a left-wing insurgent, raising the stakes in a Senate race in November that could decide overall control of the upper chamber. The question is whether the way El-Sayed has electrified the party base and tapped into their anger will work on general election voters. And whether an unabashedly left-wing Democrat can win in a swing state. The party establishment, which had backed his opponent, will hope so. Primary results across five states on Tuesday were a snapshot of the mood of the American electorate three months before the midterm elections. Here are four key takeaways from the results. 1) A new left-wing warrior Abdul El-Sayed's victory on Tuesday night in Michigan's contentious Democratic primary race for Senate was hardly a surprise. He had led by a comfortable margin over congresswoman Haley Stevens for weeks. While the final projected result was much closer than those surveys had suggested, again raising questions about modern polling accuracy, it doesn't diminish the shockwaves the victory of the former Michigan health official is sending throughout the Democratic Party. El-Sayed, the child of Egyptian immigrants, ran on a left-wing platform with the backing of such liberal stalwarts as Senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. - Left-wing political outsider wins Democratic Senate primary in Michigan - Published16 hours ago Stevens had the backing of Democratic leadership in Washington, an established record as an elected official in Michigan and deep financial pockets, including $32m from Aipac - the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Outside groups favoured her over El-Sayed by a margin of nine-to-one. None of it mattered. In debates and on the stump, El-Sayed proved to be the more gifted candidate, and Democrats seemed open to his policies, including government-sponsored health insurance, efforts to lower drug costs, higher taxes on the wealthy and campaign finance reform. His campaign refrain - "money out of politics, money in your pocket" - has been a common one among left-wing candidates this election cycle. This sets up a general election contest against former Republican congressman Mike Rogers, who ran unopposed. It will provide perhaps the most dramatic, high-stakes test of whether a left-wing candidate can win a general election race in a true battleground state. Given the narrowness of El-Sayed's primary victory, he has considerable work ahead if he wants to unite the party before November's vote. While El-Sayed did well with higher-educated liberals, he'll need to win over the lower-income voters who backed Stevens in Detroit and in more rural areas. These are voters whose preferences the pre-election polling did not seem to adequately reflect. If El-Sayed loses to Rogers, it would be a major blow to Democratic hopes of retaking control of the US Senate given a Republican hasn't won a Senate race in the state since 1994. If he wins, however, it could provide left-wing Democrats with proof of concept for why a left-wing candidate for president in 2028 could be more successful than the kind of establishment centrists the party has nominated in recent contests. And with Michigan's position as a key early state on the Democratic presidential primary calendar, the state will have an outsized say in who the party's nominee will be. 2) Some pro-Israel Democrats had a bad night Stevens was the highest-profile Aipac-backed candidate to lose on Tuesday night. In lesser-watched races, the results were more mixed. Elsewhere in Michigan, Democratic Socialist Donavan McKinney beat incumbent Shri Thanedar, who has been an outspoken supporter of continued US support for Israel. He became the latest party House incumbent to be ousted in the primaries. William Lawrence, who has called for an immediate end to US arms sales to Israel, defeated two centrist Democrats in a House of Representatives district in Michigan that is likely to be a key electoral battleground in November. If the mood of the Democratic voters has soured on pro-Israel politicians in Michigan, and in previous races in New York and Colorado, that was not the case in the Missouri and Washington results. In Washington, congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who supports military aid for Israel, easily turned away a left-wing challenger. She is one of the few Democratic incumbents in districts Trump won in 2024 - and will be a prime target for Republicans in November. Meanwhile, in a solidly liberal Missouri district, Wesley Bell denied a comeback bid from Cori Bush, a founding member of the "squad" of left-wing congresswomen. Two years ago, he unseated her in part because of her criticism of Israel. 3) Voters reject Republican measures in the Midwest While most of the contests on Tuesday night were intraparty primary fights, there were a couple of notable votes that could provide evidence that the overall mood of the electoral continues to tilt toward the Democrats. In Missouri, voters overwhelmingly rejected a ballot measure that would have made citizen-backed amendments to the state constitution more difficult to enact. In recent years, such citizen-driven efforts have been used to push Democratic initiatives that had no chance of passage in the Republican-controlled state legislature. They include protecting abortion rights and raising the minimum wage. Meanwhile in Kansas, voters rejected a ballot measure that would have have required the state's supreme court justices to stand for election. At the moment, they are appointed by the governor and a commission of lawyers. In 2024, the state high court had ruled that the right to abortion was protected by the Kansas constitution - a decision Republicans said was out-of-step with the will of state voters. Both efforts were pushed by state Republicans and, in both cases, the proposals were easily defeated. 4) Trump's endorsement still (mostly) matters It was largely a good night for Trump-backed Republicans, who earned a few victories in their primaries. John James won Michigan's Republican nomination for governor despite being heavily outspent by his wealthy opponent. Trump not only endorsed James but appeared on stage with him last week. In Kansas, Republicans opted for the Trump favourite for governor amidst a crowded field. And in the Washington state race to replace outgoing Republican congressman Dan Newhouse, Amanda McKinney, the president's pick, also finished first. The 71-year-old Newhouse, who is retiring, was notable for being one of the last two remaining House Republicans to have voted to impeach Trump after the 6 January 2021 riot at the US Capitol. Given that this is a reliably conservative district, McKinney is a favourite to defeat her Democratic opponent in November, which would likely move House Republicans further to the right. It's the latest bit of evidence that old-line establishment Republicans like Newhouse are a vanishing breed. But Trump didn't get it all his own way. In Michigan, Thomas Smith defeated Trump-endorsed Amir Hassan, a former law-enforcement officer who also appeared on stage with the president, despite Smith having dropped out of the race last month while remaining on the ballot. item.title: 'My grandmother subjected my baby to female genital mutilation behind my back'

'My grandmother subjected my baby to female genital mutilation behind my back' - Published Warning: This story contains descriptions of the practices involved in female genital mutilation In what activists are calling a milestone, Colombia last week became the first country in Latin America where female genital mutilation (FGM) is now illegal. As José Carlos Cueto reports, while the bill was passed unanimously in Colombia's Congress, it follows a long battle to eradicate the dangerous and often secretive procedure. Carla Quiñonez's daughter was just six months old when the baby's great-grandmother subjected her to female genital mutilation (FGM). Quiñonez (not her real name) says when her grandmother returned the baby to her, she had a fever and was swollen and bleeding. She cried constantly. "I confronted my grandmother, but she said it was normal and that I could not tell anyone." The nearest health centre was a long journey away, so Quiñonez's mother, a midwife, tried to ease the baby's pain with medicinal plants. She also challenged Quiñonez's grandmother. But the older woman would not listen. "She said that men make fun of women who have a clitoris." FGM in Colombia FGM involves the partial or total removal of the external female genitalia, as well as other injuries inflicted on those organs for non-medical reasons. It can cause medical complications, including haemorrhaging and infection, as well as complications later in life with periods and during childbirth. It can also make it difficult for a woman to experience sexual pleasure. The World Health Organization says that around the world more than 230 million girls and women alive today have been cut, predominantly in Africa. Quiñonez, 30, has been campaigning to eradicate the practice in Colombia - where it is still practised by members of her Emberá Indigenous community. Along with fellow activists and members of Colombia's Congress, she played a key role in the campaign which led to the ban. She says it was only as she grew up that she realised what was secretly happening within her community. "I always wondered why more girls than boys seemed to die shortly after birth. "I remember a young cousin of mine whose birth was attended by my mother. She was born healthy, but died three days later. "I asked my mother about it, and she told me the baby had died from 'jai', an ancestral illness." Quiñonez now believes that girls who supposedly died from "jai" actually died from complications related to FGM. A paediatrician's perspective Between 2020 and June 2026, 240 cases of FGM were recorded in Colombia. In the vast majority of instances, the girls were younger than six years old. But paediatrician Diana Ramos Mosquera says she believes this is just "the tip of the iceberg". Working at San Jorge University Hospital in Pereira, a city in Colombia's north-west coffee-growing region, she says she's seen signs of scarring, burning and mutilation when examining girls who have come in with other medical conditions. She recalls one girl who arrived with her vaginal opening sealed shut, meaning she probably would not have been able to menstruate or have sexual intercourse when she reached adulthood. "She had to undergo reconstructive surgery," Dr Ramos says. She regards FGM as a form of sexual and gender-based violence with lifelong consequences, but says this must be addressed through education, and not just punishment. "Some members of these communities genuinely believe they are doing no harm," she says. 'Culture does not kill' With around 300,000 members, the Great Emberá Nation is one of Colombia's largest Indigenous communities, with populations also living in Ecuador and Panama. One theory about why members of the community practise FGM, when it's rarely seen elsewhere in Latin America, is that the practice arrived with enslaved people from African countries. This could help explain its prevalence in Risaralda, Chocó and Valle del Cauca, neighbouring departments that either are home to, or border, large Afro-Colombian populations. Another theory is that the birth of an intersex child, hundreds of years ago, left the community with a fear of the clitoris - with many older women believing that it will grow into a penis if not cut. Others think that it stems from the patriarchal belief that a woman with an organ associated with sexual pleasure is more likely to be promiscuous. Whatever its origin, Juliana Domico, the legal representative and chief Indigenous councillor to the National Confederation of the Peoples of the Great Emberá Nation of Colombia, rejects the idea that the practice is cultural. "Our culture is our clothing, our crafts, our dances and our language, not a practice that kills. Culture does not kill." She says the new law follows years of advocacy work within the community: "We hope the law is translated into public policy, with sufficient resources to implement it." Threats and hostility Quiñonez is one of those who have advocated for change, but says she has received threats because of this - especially from men. While, traditionally, men are not meant to know about the ritual, conversations about abolishing the practice often only take place with male leaders because many Emberá women speak an indigenous language - also called Emberá - and have not necessarily learned Spanish. This can also prevent women from accessing help from doctors for their babies, a problem which Quiñonez says is compounded when they're faced by sometimes ill-informed and judgmental health staff. She says when she took her daughter to hospital with a fever caused by a urinary tract infection, the nurse berated her for "being a savage" and told her that she had got what she deserved. "I was even threatened with having my daughter taken away and placed in the care of the child welfare authorities. "Since then, I prefer not to take my daughter to hospital. I treat her with medicinal plants and medication. I never leave her side." 'Conversation cannot be avoided' Quiñonez says that there is change under way within the Emberá community, with women now discussing among themselves whether FGM should happen. She says she was moved when one grandmother reflected on carrying out FGM on her granddaughters. "She said she had never acted out of malice and had only wanted to prevent men from criticising her granddaughters." Having conversations about a different way of life can be painful, she says. "Women who have grown up without a clitoris cannot imagine a different body." It will also be difficult to speak to her own daughter about it, one day in the future, "but it is a conversation that cannot be avoided," she says. "All of us deserve to understand our bodies and to talk about them without shame." item.title: The avalanche that killed a climbing legend - and a generation of record-setting guides
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2ge4dnj80o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The avalanche that killed a climbing legend - and a generation of record-setting guides - Published Altogether, they summited Mount Everest dozens of times and achieved numerous feats previously thought impossible - like climbing 8,000m peaks without supplemental oxygen and scaling K2, one of the world's most lethal mountains, in the dead of winter. But beyond these accomplishments, the six Nepalis who died in an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak last week also elevated the world's recognition of Nepali mountain guides, or Sherpas, who had previously been seen as mere aides. Among those killed was the decorated British-Nepali climber Nirmal Purja, best known for climbing the world's 14 highest peaks, rising above 8,000m (26,246 ft), in just over six months. Their fellow guides say their deaths deal a devastating blow to Nepal's mountaineering community. 'Best of his generation' Purja, 43, also known as Nims, was the leading figure of the 10-member international team up Broad Peak, the world's 12th highest mountain, when the avalanche struck. "Nims of course was iconic and undisputedly amongst the best of his generation," says Ben Ayers, a longtime Everest reporter for Outside Magazine. Kili Pemba Sherpa and Pur Bahadur Gurung, who were also guiding the Broad Peak expedition, were "strong climbers with a solid resume", Ayers said. Kili Pemba, 46, had just earned the coveted mountaineering Grand Slam after completing his last of the 14 highest peaks, also known as eight-thousanders, in early July. Even before this crowning achievement, he was already among the best in the industry having been part of the Nepali team, led again by Purja, that completed the first winter ascent of K2 in January 2021. At the time, K2, the world's second highest peak, was the only one of the eight-thousanders not yet climbed in winter. But at 8,611m, K2 is known to be steeper, more unpredictable and deadlier than Everest (8,849m). Many have described Kili Pemba as humble and deeply committed in serving his clients. He'd led two double-leg amputees, on separate occasions, to the summits of Everest and Manaslu, the eighth-highest mountain. "That was the toughest task for any guide, [Kili Pemba] did that with a lot of care," says Gyanendra Shrestha, a government official who was at Everest Base Camp during one of these climbs. Pur Bahadur Gurung, 37, scaled 12 of the 14 highest peaks and was one of only 100 Nepali guides certified by the International Federation of Mountain Guides Association (IFMGA). "It takes a lot of money, passion and dedication to become an IFMGA guide. This tells us a lot about Pur Bahadur's zeal for mountaineering," says Himal Gautam, a spokesman for Nepal's tourism department. "It also speaks to the unprecedented loss we have suffered on Broad Peak," he adds. In 2024, Pur Bahadur was part of the team that discovered a century-old boot on Everest, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on the mountain in 1924. The other three Nepali guides who perished on Broad Peak last week include Gyaljen Sherpa, best known for scaling the third-highest mountain Kanchenjunga three times in one season – a feat that some colleagues say deserves a Guinness World Record. Then there's Nima Sherpa, 36, who scaled four eight-thousanders in 2026 alone, and Nawang Thindu Sherpa, who in his 20s was among Nepal's rising generation of mountain guides. Placing Pakistan on the climbing radar Nepal's mountain guides spend each spring leading international clients up Nepal's highest mountains as guides or porters. When the monsoon comes around from June to September, some of them head towards Pakistan's far north, home to some of the world's highest peaks, including five eight-thousanders. International visitors to this rugged region are relatively few, but demand is growing. While over a million adventure travellers go to the Himalayas each year, the Karakoram mountains in Pakistan attract only about 15,000 hikers annually. Some credit Purja for bringing Pakistan onto the radar of mountaineers through his feat of scaling the 14 peaks in just over six months, which was documented in a Netflix film. "Nims' success gave many [guides] and foreigners the courage to believe that this mountaineering crown was truly possible," says Iswari Paudel, acting president of the Nepal Mountaineering Association. "This has made Pakistan a major overseas base for Nepali Sherpas. And while helping foreign climbers fulfil their dreams, many guides have themselves completed the 14 peaks," Iswari says. Ayers, the Everest reporter, says Purja helped "publicise a new era of mountaineering" which in many ways helped "democratise mountain-climbing", but also "fuelled commercialisation and risk". Because of how remote Pakistan's mountains are, it is far more challenging to organise expeditions there – a feat that only the best guides undertake, Sherpas tell the BBC. "We have to fix our own ropes, cut our steps into the ice, and set up camps as we go along," says Nima Rinji Sherpa. The 20-year-old set a new record in 2024 as the youngest mountaineer to summit the world's 14 highest peaks. "Even in an era of commercial mountaineering, we experience real, old-fashioned mountaineering [in Pakistan]," he says. But because the region is hard to access, climbers usually attempt two to three mountains per trip, which makes the itinerary very tight, Nima Rinji adds. In Nepal, by contrast, mountaineering infrastructure is well-developed. The main trekking routes towards Everest are lined with family-run lodges that offer beds, hot meals and other facilities. Emergency evacuations are also generally easier in the Himalayas, where there is an integrated network of rescue helicopters and aid outposts at high altitude, whereas the Karakoram range, being more isolated, features fewer accessible landing zones. "In the Pakistan mountains, getting the helicopters to base camp already takes a lot more effort, let alone flying them above high camps. "Therefore, the Sherpas who are capable of working in high-pressure situations, and who have diverse experiences and multiple skills are the ones who will operate in Pakistan," Nima Rinji says. The risks are part of the appeal While the Broad Peak disaster may spur calls to tighten safety standards, many believe it will do little to change high-altitude tourism. "Generally, these tragedies cause a moment of concern... but then things go back to how they were. It's difficult to say with any conviction that any accident in the mountains is 'preventable' as the inherent danger is so high... and that's part of the appeal," Ayers says. The mountaineering community is drawn to high-risk pursuits, says Medhavi Gulati, a researcher specialising in high-altitude mountaineering. "Often, it's the dangers and risk of death that attracts people," she says. The existing generation of mountain guides will continue to crave the global fame and world records that their predecessors have attained, she says. "I don't think that appeal will ever go away," she says. "We've seen disasters like this one before, and nothing changed," says expert mountaineer and writer Alan Arnette, who pointed to how an ice avalanche on Everest killed 16 Sherpas in April 2014, and the 11 climbers who died on K2 in 2008 after a massive chunk of ice broke off. "I doubt the Broad Peak incident will have a significant impact, given history. I hope I'm wrong," he says. Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. item.title: 'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transition
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgr7nxve05go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transition - Published For 15 years, single mother Lisa made a living from content writing. She began writing straight out of college, freelanced for years and eventually followed a path taken by many young Filipinos: joining a multinational in the country's booming outsourcing industry. Lisa says she never felt the need to use artificial intelligence (AI) in her work. "I can say that I am able to do my job, I meet deadlines. In my opinion, there is no need for [AI]," she told the BBC. Eight months into her latest role, and one month before the position was due to become permanent, she was made redundant. In the months before, Lisa says a public relations agency had been tasked with producing AI-generated material that she and her colleagues were asked to edit. She says her skills were used to train the AI on the company writing style. "I feel like I dug my own grave," she says. "We were the ones who trained the artificial intelligence that replaced us." Lisa, not her real name, is one of several former outsourcing employees the BBC spoke to who asked to remain anonymous. They signed confidentiality agreements in return for severance pay, and fear that speaking publicly could hurt their chances of finding work in an industry which has a small network. Their experiences offer an insight into a question confronting emerging economies like the Philippines: what happens when AI begins to automate the jobs that helped lift millions of people into the middle classes? Building an industry Every evening around 5pm, streams of workers wearing company lanyards spill out of high-rise offices in the district of Cubao in Manila. It's one of several areas of the capital where multinational companies have premises – providing all sorts of outsourcing work including call centres, accounting, software development and marketing copy services for clients thousands of miles away. For over two decades, these business districts have symbolised one of the Philippines' biggest economic success stories. Beginning in the early 2000s, the country was promoted as an English-speaking alternative to India for what's called business process outsourcing (BPO). Successive governments offered tax incentives, invested in infrastructure and encouraged multinational companies to set up large operations. Global groups like Accenture, Concentrix and Teleperformance built sprawling campuses, employing hundreds of thousands of Filipinos. Today, the outsourcing industry employs roughly 1.9 million people, and generates $40bn (£30.1bn) in revenues every year, accounting for about 10% of the Philippines' economy. But experts say the industry is disproportionately vulnerable to the impact of AI. The International Labour Organization estimates that 12.7 million Filipinos - more than one in four workers - are employed in occupations exposed to generative AI, the highest share in South East Asia. The organisation expects many roles to change rather than disappear but the types of service jobs that people do in the Philippines leaves it particularly at risk. Jack Madrid, president of the IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines (IBPAP), admits that AI is being adopted by the sector. More than two-thirds of IBPAP's members are already running AI pilots, he says. "Agentic AI has the potential to automate at a much more accelerated pace," Madrid says. "Obviously, there's a layer of jobs that are automatable or have been automated." But he adds that the vast majority of affected workers have been redeployed within the same organisations. Madrid says any weakness in hiring reflects more than the impact of AI. "We've seen a slowdown in investment decisions on whether certain job functions or processes should be offshored," he says, pointing to slower global demand and uncertainty over how companies will ultimately deploy the technology. Even so, he acknowledges the challenge. "We cannot do enough to be prepared," he says. "The importance of reskilling" cannot be overstated. The pressure to automate Mary, another former content writer whose name we've changed, says her employer encouraged the use of AI as a productivity tool. Instead of making her job easier, she says it created additional responsibilities. "We had to edit more, fact-check more because the data AI produced was inaccurate," she says. "Technically it was more work for us." Like Lisa, she was later made redundant. Companies are under pressure to implement AI, to reduce costs and increase productivity, experts say. Teleperformance, the world's largest call centre operator and one of the Philippines' biggest private employers, has said AI offers an opportunity to augment rather than replace its workforce. The company expects AI to handle routine interactions while human agents move into more complex roles. Teleperformance has also said it plans to retrain employees. Accenture has similarly said that generative AI will reshape almost every job rather than eliminate positions. The firm has promised to invest billions of dollars in AI capabilities and workforce training. Concentrix - which is the biggest outsourcing firm in the Philippines - says its AI systems should remain under human oversight and has committed to training employees in the new technology. Some Filipino managers are uneasy about AI and want to slow down adoption, according to Paul Quintos, from the University of the Philippines-Diliman. They are concerned about how much of the domestic workforce might be displaced. "But there's tremendous pressure from foreign clients to adopt AI," he says. "It's a major cost-cutting measure." Philippine outsourcing companies compete directly with rivals in India and elsewhere for contracts from multinational corporations. Increasingly, those clients expect suppliers not only to provide cheaper labour, but also to integrate AI into the services they deliver. Despite hundreds of billions of dollars being invested globally in AI, Quintos says there is still limited evidence about how much productivity many workplace tools actually deliver. "There is a term called 'AI washing'," he says. Some layoffs are presented as being driven by AI when companies are in fact responding to weaker demand or slowing economic conditions, Quintos says. Attributing redundancies to AI, he adds, can make restructuring appear like technological progress rather than a response to market conditions. The next transition Labour groups have told the BBC that existing employment laws in the Philippines govern redundancy but offer little guidance on how companies should introduce AI into workplaces or consult employees over its use. The Philippines' outsourcing sector is also non-unionised, leaving many workers with little formal say over how new technologies are deployed. The government says that it, and the private sector have a responsibility to retrain workers, and risks falling behind competitors like India and Singapore. "To be completely honest, I think we're slightly behind. We have to catch up," says Leandro Aguirre of the Philippines Department of Information and Communications Technology. "We have to double our efforts to put our people in a position where they will not be displaced but actually thrive in this growing AI race." The government has committed to upskilling more than 300,000 outsourcing workers, but Aguirre acknowledges that the Philippines may need to rethink the economic model that helped make it an outsourcing centre. "We relied heavily on foreign direct investment," he says. "But I think we also need to focus on local talent and local companies." The ambition, he says, is to build home-grown AI companies capable of creating higher-value jobs. Aguirre rejects calls for sweeping new AI legislation, arguing that existing labour, privacy and consumer protection laws can be adapted more quickly through regulatory guidance. "The benefits of AI have to trickle down to people," he says. "It can't just benefit employers." For more than 20 years, the Philippines built one of the world's most successful outsourcing industries by selling the skills of its people to multinational companies. AI may not end that model, but it is certainly changing it, and risks leaving some workers behind. Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar and Regine Cabato

item.title: 'I was slut-shamed' - Indian women 'cockroach' protesters doxxed and abused
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g43l251vyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'I was slut-shamed' - Indian women 'cockroach' protesters doxxed and abused - Published Their videos lasted only a few seconds: lip-syncs, sarcastic reels and jokes filmed on the way to protests. But while thousands of young people filled social media with memes and videos mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi during one of India's biggest anti-government protest in years, many of the women behind those posts say they have paid a heavy price for speaking out. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led movement that helped force the resignation of India's education minister, relied as much on Instagram as it did on marches. Memes, reels and viral videos became the movement's calling card, documenting everything from protest songs to the police crackdown when officers used tear gas and baton charges to stop demonstrators marching to parliament on 20 July. Delhi police said 60 protesters and 118 police personnel were injured on the day, but the CJP said the number of injured protesters was significantly higher than the official count. The posts reached hundreds of thousands of people, turning ordinary students into some of the movement's most recognisable faces. Since the protests ended, police have opened criminal cases against some protesters. But many women say another reckoning played out online. They describe rape threats, doctored images spreading on social media and strangers trawling through their photos and videos. Some cases spilled into TV debates, police complaints and political statements. Many more unfolded quietly, as young women deleted posts, locked their accounts and stopped answering calls from unknown numbers. The BBC spoke to four women and reviewed screenshots of abusive messages, posts and other material they shared. Their names have not been used to protect their identities. Content creator I'm in my mid-20s. I had been posting about the protests from the beginning, but 20 July was the first time I attended one. After the baton charge that day and the internet shutdown around the protest site, I went home and started sharing first-person accounts on Instagram. I also helped organise food, aid and volunteers. I thought I was just helping and didn't think of it as political. But the hate started almost immediately. I was slut-shamed and I was attacked for questioning the prime minister's comments, external after the protest ended. [Modi said he forgave the children who had abused him, urging society to do the same rather than punish them or drag them through the courts.] I have lost count of the number of messages I have deleted and people I have blocked. But the comments keep coming. As a content creator, I already live with this feeling of constantly being watched. Every word I say is scrutinised, mostly by men. When I first started creating content, I would block men if they made me feel uncomfortable. Over time, the algorithm started pushing my content towards more women. I believe that has shielded me from abuse compared with many other female creators. And still, this happened. My mother stopped reading the comments on my posts long ago. She said she couldn't bear the things strangers were saying about her daughter. I understood. What parent wouldn't be frightened by that? As a woman in India, you grow up with fear. You're told not to stay out late, to watch where you go, who you're with and how you'll get home. You learn early that your safety is something you must constantly think about. When you have a voice online, that fear doesn't disappear. It just follows you there. College student I am 20 years old, and this was my first protest. I went because I believed the students were standing up for something important. Before leaving the Metro station, I propped my phone against a railing and filmed a quick "fit check" [a video showing off her outfit before the protest.] "Going to get beaten by cops, guys," I joked. That's the kind of light-hearted videos I usually make. When police fired tear gas and charged protesters that afternoon, I kept filming. I was simply recording what was happening around me, as I always do. I never imagined those videos would reach far beyond my followers. I was wrong. One of them was shown on a national TV channel. Soon afterwards, my face began appearing in social media posts claiming protesters were being identified by the police. Someone even found out which college I attended. That's when I realised people weren't just attacking me online. They were trying to find me. My inbox filled with anonymous messages. Some said they would report me to the police so I would be beaten or arrested. Men called me degrading names associated with prostitution, made sexually explicit remarks, mocked my body and threatened violence. Some said I should be "taught a lesson". Others simply warned: "Your turn will come." What frightened me most wasn't the abuse itself, but what followed. Relatives and acquaintances called my parents, urging them to make me delete my videos or face the consequences. Seeing them so frightened was devastating. That's why I don't want my name published. I've since removed or archived almost all my protest videos. I worry less about what could happen to me than what they might do to my parents. Student activist I have always spoken my mind online. I'm a student activist and a Muslim, part of a religious minority in an increasingly polarised India. None of that ever frightened me. But after the CJP protests, everything changed. My Instagram account is private now. I've muted most of my other social media because the abuse has been unrelenting. Every time I look at my phone, there's another offensive comment or message or post about me. I went to the protest because I believed it was the right thing to do. I made a few satirical videos during the march. One mocked the prime minister. Others showed us singing on stage and chanting slogans. They were political, irreverent and the kind of videos I'd always made. But they spread far beyond the people I knew. One Instagram page edited a photograph to make it appear as though I was kissing a man to shame me. Another morphed my images and branded me an anti-national and a terrorist. I was also called a hijra - using the term for South Asia's transgender community as an insult - and dismissed as a paid protester. When my father, a journalist, read the comments, he panicked. He kept asking why I had spoken out. He said that once people saw my Muslim name, nothing else would matter. My parents have watched other Muslim activists investigated and arrested, and fear the same could happen to me. We live under constant dread. But I'm not going to stop speaking up. I still believe I was right to go to that protest. Now I just understand the cost much better than I did before. Student I'm a student in [the state of] West Bengal, where political discussions are an integral part of college life. I've participated in those conversations on campus for years, so I didn't think much before posting online about the protests. Although I first joined the Kolkata protest on 20 July, I'd already been helping online, organising supplies ranging from diabetic biscuits to masks for people worried about being identified. A friend and I also launched an Instagram fundraiser. But on 24 July, the police started detaining protesters in the state and we began talking about it online. That's when the hate really started. People began leaving spiteful comments on my fundraiser post; they called me a prostitute in private messages. They did not stop even after the protest had ended - and eventually I deleted the post. In the days that followed, the fear of being doxxed became real. I changed my name on social media, made my account private and blocked messages from people I didn't know. What hurt most was that none of my male friends faced the abuse I did. They expressed similar views but weren't targeted over their sexuality or subjected to insults about their mothers. I was. When it comes to women, the response quickly becomes about our gender. That's left me wondering why women can't express the same opinions as men online.

Umit is one of four Amur tigers transferred from Russia. She will be monitored on how she takes to the new habitat before a decision is made on when to release the other three. Record heatwave in South Korea as temperatures soar to 42.5C South Korea is struggling against the effects of a blistering heatwave which has brought its highest ever temperatures. A high of 42.5C was recorded on Sunday in the southern city of Yangsan, the country's highest temperature since modern record keeping began. At least 19 people have died during the heatwave, according to authorities, and Seoul is under a severe heat warning for the first time under a system established this year by the government to respond to rising temperatures. Ukrainian vegetable seller targeted in 'human safari' drone attack Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared a video of a street vendor being hunted by a drone before it exploded. The man in the video verified by the BBC, 52-year-old street vegetable seller Yuriy, managed to survive the attack, but sustained shrapnel wounds and a concussion. Known by some in Ukraine as "human safari", the deployment of remotely-operated drones against civilians has often been used by Russians to terrify residents of front line areas. This particular drone attack happened in Kherson, which sits only a few miles from the front line. Russia has repeatedly denied intentionally targeting civilians. The BBC's Paul Adams reports from Kyiv.
